name: Tawny Orange
lede: Tawny orange is an old descriptive pairing of two color words, tawny and orange, for a warm brown-orange close to amber.

sections.title: Tawny and orange
sections.body:
*Tawny* is an old word for a dark brown tied to birds and animals, from the French *tanné*, meaning tan [1]. Paterson also records a Greek combining form, *cirrho-*, glossed as tawny or orange [2]. The pair is a modifier and a noun and not a separate invention, which makes the name's origin undocumented as a single coinage.

The phrase turns up in Werner's color nomenclature as used by physicians [3]. In a table Baty reproduces, a medical color list puts "tawny orange" beside a gloss of amber yellow, evidence that early nineteenth-century doctors used Werner's names to describe the body [3]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas and the ISCC-NBS list of 1955 both carry the name in our library [4]. Nearby named colors are [[tawny]], [[amber]] and [[orange-brown]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color near Tawny Orange appears in 931 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 3.91 per cent, more common than 87 per cent of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 65 paintings, 2.1 times the expected rate, and Bellini has it in 6 of 17 works [5]. It usually plays an accent, in 71 per cent of 767 paintings [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings; nothing here shows what pigment made the color.
